# Vectors in Postgres

![](../images/spot-2.svg){.spot fig-alt="A grid of white towers on a lime tile, with a violet ball floating above the yellow-topped one. An elephant in a lab coat inspects them with a magnifying glass."}
With [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector), semantic search is an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`
on the table that already holds the text, its permissions and its foreign keys, so there is no second
store to keep in sync. The lab's doc-search app retrieves from 407 chunks of the SQLAlchemy
documentation this way in about 20 ms. The work lies in the indexes, which return slightly wrong
answers by design and are easy to bypass without noticing.

## Each distance needs its own opclass

pgvector adds a `vector` type and four distance operators, and each operator needs its own index
operator class (opclass):

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | what it is | index opclass |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a <-> b` | `col.l2_distance(b)` | Euclidean distance | `vector_l2_ops` |
| `a <=> b` | `col.cosine_distance(b)` | 1 minus the cosine: 0 same direction, 2 opposite | `vector_cosine_ops` |
| `a <#> b` | `col.max_inner_product(b)` | the negative inner product (so smaller is closer) | `vector_ip_ops` |
| `a <+> b` | `col.l1_distance(b)` | taxicab distance | `vector_l1_ops` |

Most embedding models produce vectors of length 1, and for those cosine and inner product put
results in the same order, with inner product skipping a division. The notebook starts with a dozen
hand-made three-dimensional vectors whose axes mean something (`[fruit, tech, sport]`), so each
distance can be predicted before Postgres computes it.

## A similarity query is an ordinary SELECT

Filters, joins and labels go around the distance as in any other query:

```python
distance = Document.embedding.cosine_distance(query_vec).label("distance")
stmt = (
    select(Document.title, distance)
    .where(Document.category == "orm")  # ordinary filters first
    .order_by(distance)
    .limit(5)
)
```

Most production search adds a rerank. A CTE takes the top 50 by vector distance, and the outer query
orders those 50 by a blended score, such as similarity with popularity or recency, or by a
cross-encoder. For the top k per group, `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY distance)`
numbers the rows within each category, and the query keeps the first three of each.

## Re-embedding is one upsert

Embedding pipelines run again whenever the source text changes, and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO
UPDATE` on a unique key inserts new rows and refreshes existing ones in one statement:

```python
stmt = insert(Document).values(rows)
stmt = stmt.on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["name"], set_={"embedding": stmt.excluded.embedding})
```

## An index changes the answer

Without an index, Postgres computes the distance to every row and sorts them, which is exact and
affordable up to some tens of thousands of rows. An approximate nearest-neighbor index is much
faster but *slightly wrong*, and how wrong is a setting.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The opclass must match the operator

An HNSW index built with `vector_l2_ops` is ignored by a query that orders by `<=>`. The plan
quietly goes back to a sequential scan. Check with `EXPLAIN` after each index change.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Filters run after the walk

HNSW collects `hnsw.ef_search` candidates first and applies `WHERE` afterwards. A filter that keeps
10% of rows throws most candidates away, and the query can return fewer rows than its `LIMIT`.
pgvector 0.8 added iterative scans, which keep walking the graph until the limit is met. Turn them
on with `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order`.
:::

## The doc-search app

The lab's FastAPI app uses these queries for its doc search. `app/ingest.py` fetches 20 pages of the
SQLAlchemy documentation, splits them by section into chunks of about 250 words, embeds each chunk
with `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384 dimensions, ONNX on the CPU) and stores the 407 rows with an
HNSW index.

`POST /ask` embeds the question, takes the five chunks closest by cosine distance, and builds an
extractive summary from their sentences, so nothing is generated and each answer carries its
sources. Retrieval takes about 20 ms, and the [sync and async scene](sqlalchemy.qmd#watching-it-happen)
shows those queries in flight, with the chunks laid out by a PCA of their real embeddings.

::: {.chapter-notebook}
The measurements come from the [pgvector notebook](../notebooks/pgvector_playground.ipynb), run on
pg18, which also holds the index comparison of the next chapter.
:::
